title: White House reverses a 17-day freeze and restores Britain’s AI Security Institute access to pre-release OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepMind models
summary: As of Sunday, October 11, the White House has reinstated the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) access to pre-release frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, The Telegraph reports (via AOL and CryptoBriefing). On September 24 the Trump administration’s Office of the National Cyber Director had asked OpenAI and Anthropic to stop sharing new models with AISI pending a U.S. national security review; the freeze lasted 17 days. During it, Anthropic kept Claude Mythos 5.1 out of UK review and limited it to U.S. organizations. The reversal followed lobbying by UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan. AISI was set up after the 2023 AI safety summit to evaluate advanced systems before public release. Whether the national security review is finished, and whether Anthropic will broaden Mythos 5.1 beyond U.S. access, remains unclear.

title: Anthropic pauses free Claude Team and $1,000 API credits for Startups after applications jumped 21× in 48 hours
summary: Anthropic has paused the free year of Claude Team (up to five users) and $1,000 API-credit offers in its expanded Claude Startups program after a surge of hundreds of thousands of applications, Forbes reports via Yahoo Tech. The expansion launched Tuesday as part of SF Tech Week; Sarah Wolf, Anthropic’s head of startup marketing, said on X Thursday night that the first 48 hours brought 21 times as many applications as the prior five months, that acceptance criteria were not tuned, and that many non-startups got in. Founders who already claimed the offers keep them; unclaimed approvals are being re-verified and some may lose access. Startup Stack discounts (up to about $45,000), Applied AI office hours, and events remain. Wolf apologized and said Anthropic is working to restore access for qualified startups.

title: S&P 500 rises 0.59% and the Nasdaq 0.64% into earnings week after Friday’s rebound
summary: U.S. markets were closed over the weekend; the last session was Friday, October 9, when all three major indexes rose and logged weekly gains, Reuters reports: the S&P 500 gained 46.15 points, or 0.59%, to 7,811.51, the Nasdaq Composite added 172.83 points, or 0.64%, to 27,366.17, and the Dow rose 423.31 points, or 0.83%, to 51,654.95. AI-related momentum stocks were generally higher, with the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF up 1%. Communication services was the only S&P 500 sector to fall; T-Mobile US, AT&T, and Verizon dropped between 8.8% and 13.3% after SpaceX struck a deal for a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio, and Apple slid 1.1% after a report that it told some suppliers to cut iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max component production. Third-quarter earnings season begins in earnest this week with the big banks, and inflation data is due. GROKI does not print live share prices.

title: Bears pile into chip puts on Friday, including a $21 million bet against Nvidia
summary: Bears kept building positions against semiconductor stocks on Friday, October 9, CNBC reports. More than 180,000 puts traded in the SMH chip ETF by midday, against 50,000 calls, with $46 million of premium tied to puts versus $26 million in calls, according to ThinkOrSwim and SpotGamma data, and the ratio of open put contracts to calls climbed to 1.95, its highest since the second week of August, Barchart data show. In Nvidia, just after the opening bell, someone bought 100,000 puts at the 180 strike expiring January 15 for $21 million, the biggest trade in the stock’s options that day; as a speculative position, it would need Nvidia to fall 22% by expiry. Nvidia closed Friday at $229.28, down 0.52% on the day and about 2.0% for the week. In Micron, about $270 million of premium was tied to likely put-buying, including deep in-the-money puts expiring in June 2028. CNBC cautions that reading such trades from bid-ask spreads can get murky. GROKI does not print live share prices.

title: Anthropic clears the Claude Code Projects waitlist for Pro and Max users, spinning one chat into parallel task threads
summary: Anthropic’s ClaudeDevs account said on October 9 that every Pro and Max user then on the Claude Code Projects waitlist had been admitted. Projects turn an ongoing conversation into a coordinator: Claude scopes the work, runs each task as its own parallel thread in the cloud, and assembles the results, with docs and a short walkthrough posted alongside the announcement. The feature remains in beta; new users can still join the waitlist as capacity allows, and Team and Enterprise plans are not in yet. Early users describe personal agents that sift email and Slack for automations, and warn that idle subagents can burn through usage limits quickly.

title: Microsoft-Decision-1 doesn’t write, it decides, and Microsoft clocks it at 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol
summary: Microsoft on October 9 introduced Microsoft-Decision-1, a fast “decision-scoring” model available in Microsoft Foundry and through OpenRouter. Instead of generating text, it takes a fixed set of answer options (yes/no, multiple choice, ratings, or rubric grades of AI responses and agent actions) and returns a calibrated probability for each, for jobs like routing, classification, prioritization, verification, and workflow control. Microsoft post-trained it from Qwen3.5-9B and says it will soon rebase it on other models, including Microsoft AI (MAI) and OpenAI. In Microsoft’s 36-benchmark comparison, spanning nearly 150,000 questions kept blind from training, it had the highest accuracy and was the fastest measured: 2.5 times quicker than runner-up H2O-Lightning-4B v1.1 and 35 times quicker than GPT-6 Sol. When the same request is perturbed in eight ways, it changes its decision 1.3% of the time on average. Input costs $0.042 per million tokens, and output tokens are free.

title: TypeSafe AI, maker of the non-text model Jev, raises $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation weeks after launch
summary: TypeSafe AI, the developer of Jev, has raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation in a round led by Andreessen Horowitz, with Sequoia and existing investor DCVC, TechCrunch reports. Jev went viral almost instantly after its September 15 release, and the startup claims a third of Fortune 500 companies already use it. Jev is built on a transformer architecture but is not a large language model: it doesn’t output text, and instead produces probabilities, which the company calls “calibrated decisions.” TypeSafe claims it works significantly faster and uses far fewer tokens than LLMs, and positions it for automating tasks rather than generating text or code. “We have been super good at human language for four years, but it’s not useful for automation because computers speak a different language,” co-founder Diogo Almeida, a former OpenAI researcher, told TechCrunch last month. TypeSafe was co-founded in 2024 by Almeida, former Meta research engineer Sasha Sheng, and Erik Gafni.

title: DeepMind’s AlphaProof Nexus solves dozens of open math problems and lands a peer-reviewed Science paper
summary: Google DeepMind’s AlphaProof Nexus solved dozens of open mathematics problems on its own, according to a new study in Science reported October 12 by The Decoder. It cracked nine of 353 open Erdős problems—two unsolved for 56 years—and the team shared those solutions online ahead of the paper. It also proved 44 conjectures from the OEIS integer sequence database, solved an open question in algebraic geometry, and improved a known bound in min-max optimization. The system is built around Gemini 3.1 Pro, which drafts and revises proofs in the formal language Lean; Lean checks each draft after every edit, and for harder sub-problems it can call on AlphaProof. Even without AlphaProof it solved the nine Erdős problems, DeepMind reports. The paper arrives amid debate over AI math: OpenAI recently posted hundreds of AI proofs on GitHub instead of journals, while DeepMind put its work through peer review.

title: DOE, NIH, and Biohub team up to build the open data for AI models that predict how cells behave
summary: The Department of Energy’s Office of Science, the National Institutes of Health, and Biohub signed a memorandum of understanding on October 9 to build an open biological data foundation for predictive AI models of living systems that can accurately predict how cells respond to interventions, according to DOE’s announcement. DOE is investing more than $500 million over five years in fundamental cell research spanning data collection, AI analytics, lab measurement and imaging, modeling, and computation, and Biohub is investing $500 million over five years in its Virtual Biology Initiative. The work joins DOE national labs’ exascale supercomputers and user facilities such as the Joint Genome Institute, AI-driven robotic “autonomous laboratories,” Biohub’s AI technologies, and NIH’s health data and imaging, as part of the Genesis Mission. “An accurate predictive model of biology could dramatically accelerate scientific discovery by enabling scientists to perform experiments digitally,” said Biohub head of science Alex Rives.
sourceName: U.S. Department of Energy via HPCwire

title: No computers, no internet, so an ASU student taught AI literacy in rural Kenya with storybooks instead
summary: Martin Ndegwa, an Arizona State University master’s student and Mastercard Foundation Scholar, went home to Kenya to teach AI and data literacy, ASU News reports, but found that some rural schools in Kilifi County lacked reliable electricity, computers, or internet, and for some communities the nearest library services were more than 30 kilometers away. “When you go to the field, you have to listen to what the field requires,” he says. So he pivoted: with local partners he helped set up Shomani Reading Clubs in six rural primary schools, and his team used AI to help create two illustrated printed storybooks. In “Zuri’s Big Questions,” for ages 8 to 11, a girl learns that a phone assistant sometimes helps and sometimes gives a silly answer; in “Amani and the Elephant Problem,” for ages 12 to 15, students check a confident but impractical AI answer against evidence and the advice of farmers, elders, and a wildlife ranger, then pitch a beehive-fence pilot. “Once you get an answer, the first step is to confirm what you’ve gotten,” Ndegwa says. “Is it really true?”

title: A Chicago special education teacher uses Gemini as a planning partner to get her students up and moving
summary: Cheryl Graff, a special education teacher at Lake View High School in Chicago, writes on Google’s blog that she used to struggle to bridge abstract literature concepts and true hands-on learning. Now Gemini is her planning partner: before her English classes read complex stories about climate change or human rights, it helps her quickly build multi-station role-playing simulations that let students physically move through the room to solve problems and build empathy. In her Life Skills courses, it helps design smoothie recipes and dietary profiles so students can blend ingredients and practice mindful nutrition firsthand. “Gemini isn’t a replacement for active teaching,” she writes. “It’s a tool that helps me bring movement and deeper engagement into my classroom.”

title: Yesterday’s festival finale at Girard Park: French Mass at 9, BeauSoleil at 11:30, Bayou Blues with Sonny Landreth, Wayne Toups to close
summary: Festivals Acadiens et Créoles wrapped its free weekend at Girard Park on Sunday, October 11, per Lafayette Travel’s posted schedule. The day opened with a French Mass at 9 a.m. and Danse Rondes at 10 a.m. in the Salle De Danse, which later had Jeffery Broussard & the Creole Cowboys at 5:15 p.m. Scène 76 had BeauSoleil at 11:30 a.m., Cedric Watson and Corey Harris at 2 p.m., Louis Michot, Corey Ledet & Leyla McCalla at 3:15 p.m., and at 4:30 p.m. a Bayou Blues Band with Roddie Romero, Sonny Landreth, Michael Doucet, Grant Dermody, Michael Juan Nunez, and more. Scène Mon Heritage had the Pine Leaf Boys at 1:15 p.m., Dwayne Dopsie & the Zydeco Hellraisers at 3:45 p.m., and Lost Bayou Ramblers at 5 p.m., and Wayne Toups & Friends closed Scène Ma Louisiane at 6:30 p.m.

title: Tonight at Poche’s Patch & Maze: Thursday hours 3:30 to 6 p.m. at 930 Guilbeau Road
summary: Poche’s Patch & Maze at 930 Guilbeau Road in Lafayette is open this afternoon, Monday, October 12, on its Thursday schedule of 3:30 to 6 p.m., according to the venue’s site (Thursday hours apply across its Oct. 1–Nov. 1 season; Saturday and Sunday are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.). Entry is $10 cash, plus $5 if you want a pumpkin; attractions include a giant maze, book walk, jungle bus, selfie stations, obstacle courses, culvert slides, the Tree House, Mole Hole Mountain, and Candy Corn Village. Infants are free; field trips run by appointment weekdays. The bar is open Friday through Sunday only.

title: Ragin’ Cajuns fall 32–31 at Louisiana Tech in the final seconds; Troy comes to Cajun Field Saturday
summary: Louisiana Tech edged Louisiana 32–31 on Saturday night, October 10, at Origin Bank Field in Ruston after a 19-point fourth quarter, the Ragin’ Cajuns athletics site and the AP report. Louisiana (now 4-2, 1-1 Sun Belt) led 31–19 with over 11 minutes left after Lunch Winfield’s 45-yard touchdown pass to KeDarius Wade, but Blake Baker’s 12-yard run and 7-yard touchdown pass to Eli Finley with 46 seconds left put Tech ahead; Winfield was intercepted with 19 seconds remaining. Winfield was 14-of-24 for 239 yards, a touchdown, and two interceptions. Louisiana hosts Troy on Saturday, October 17, at 4 p.m. for Hall of Fame Weekend on ESPN+.

title: Tonight, 6 to 8 p.m.: An Evening with Jessica Alexander at Cavalier House Books downtown
summary: Writer Jessica Alexander closes UL Lafayette’s 2026 Levy Humanities Series tonight, Monday, October 12, from 6 to 8 p.m. at Cavalier House Books, 302 Jefferson Street in Downtown Lafayette, per Downtown Lafayette and the university. The free reading and Q&A has limited seats; she will read from Agnes, We’re Not Murderers, with a book signing to follow. Metered street parking downtown is free after 5 p.m. on weekdays, and the Parc-Auto du Centre-Ville garage at 121 East Vermilion Street has 530 spaces.

title: Next Saturday at Moncus Park: Lafayette Farmers & Artisans Market, 8 a.m. to noon
summary: The Lafayette Farmers & Artisans Market returns Saturday, October 17, from 8 a.m. to noon at Moncus Park, 2913 Johnston Street, rain or shine, according to the park’s listing. It is a producer-only market with more than 150 vendors—just-picked produce, local honey, fresh flowers, baked goods, and handmade crafts. Parking in the park’s lot is $2 an hour, or free for Moncus Park members, with proceeds supporting the nonprofit park conservancy; park only at Moncus Park, since towing is strictly enforced in neighboring lots. The weekly vendor lineup is posted on the market’s Facebook page the Friday before.
